title: What Most Folks Get Wrong About John Hattie
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. sets out four common mistakes in how educators treat John Hattie's Visible Learning research. The first is thinking it is finished: the database now covers roughly 440 influences and 2,500 meta-analyses, and the effect size for feedback has moved from .73 to .48 as Hattie responded to statistical critiques. The second is treating the ranked list like a menu of magic spells, which buzzwordifies the work when Hattie himself wants the list to prompt questions and hypotheses. The third is thinking the numbers are the point; he cites the princesses-are-larger-than-elephants critique and says the real value lies in the story beneath the numbers, summarised as teachers seeing learning through students' eyes and students becoming their own teachers. The fourth is throwing Hattie out entirely, and he answers three further critiques, noting a University of Melbourne investigation into citation practices that he will not prejudge. He promises more exploration of Hattie on his blog.
points: Hattie's data keeps changing, so effect sizes quoted from older sources, such as the .73 for feedback now revised to .48, can be out of date.
Sorting the list by effect size and pasting the top items into PD decks turns research into buzzwords, which Hattie himself warns against.
Because pooled effect sizes can hide very different studies, the useful move is to look for mechanisms and the story behind a number rather than rank influences.
The core message he draws from Visible Learning is that learning is strongest when teachers see learning through students' eyes and students act as their own teachers.
Rejecting Hattie wholesale is also a mistake, since measuring achievement matters and responsibility for guru-style citation rests with those who cite him.
quotes: For the last 25+ years, this intrepid Kiwi colleague of ours has been trying to answer a single question: which variables have the greatest impact on student achievement?

Most notably, his effect size for feedback went from a .73 at one point to a .48. This is in part because of Hattie’s responsiveness to various critiques levied against his work on statistical and methodological grounds since Visible Learning was published almost two decades ago.

In work as hard as ours, we’re desperate for magic; and so we end up acting like if we just say “Hattie” or “Collective Teacher Efficacy” or “Teacher Clarity” or “effect size” enough times, then the magic spell will work.

Hattie himself agrees that it’s wrong to simply pull things from the top of his table and ignore the story behind the numbers. The list, properly conceived, is meant to get us to ask questions, form hypotheses, search for principles, and run experiments.

Hattie’s response, however, is one that lines up with how one can sensibly approach his numbers: the point isn’t the effect sizes and how they rank; rather, the point is to look for the story that the numbers tell, the meaning beneath the numbers, the mechanisms inside of how those numbers came to be.
Learning occurs best when 1) teachers see that learning through the eyes of their students and 2) students see themselves as their own teachers.
Measuring and aiming at mastery is in fact an essential part of the way we promote the long-term flourishing of young people.
The ultimate responsibility for turning Hattie into a blithely-followed guru rests upon each of our shoulders, not his.
